title: How many cakes for ten children, the same share as Ruhee?
description: Two cakes are shared among five children in Ruhee's group. Putting two such groups together gives ten children and four cakes, so each child gets four tenths, the same as two fifths, while Keeko doubts it by adding five more cakes.
teaching_notes: One idea: copying a whole sharing group, cakes and children together, keeps the share the same. Watch for students who add the same number to the cakes and to the children.

source: In Anil's group, 2 cakes are divided equally among 5 childre
video_script.why: The child finds how many cakes ten children need to get the same share as Ruhee, by putting two groups of two cakes and five children together.
video_script.substitution: none: the book's own cakes shared in Ruhee's group
video_script.anchor: two cakes on a table and five children in Ruhee's group
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says seven cakes, because five more children need five more cakes. With seven cakes every child would get more than Ruhee, so adding the same number does not keep the share the same.
video_script.payoff_line: Four cakes are needed, and each child gets four tenths, the same as two fifths

final_answer.spoken: four cakes, and each child gets four tenths, the same as two fifths

names.Ruhee: the child who gets two fifths of a cake when two cakes are shared among five children

maths_rules: Ruhee's group: 2 cakes shared equally among 5 children, so each child gets 2/5 of a cake
each group of 5 needs 2 cakes, so 2 groups need 2 + 2 = 4 cakes
4 cakes among 10 children: each child gets 4/10 of a cake, the same as 2/5
slip: Keeko thinks 7 cakes, adding 5 to the cakes because 5 more children; 7 cakes among 10 is 7/10, more than 2/5
video_script.design: One idea: copy the whole group, cakes and children together. The first group stays on the table and a second identical group is placed beside it.

beats.on_screen: small title card From your book; two cakes on a table with five children around them, a second group of ten children waiting at another table

marks.scene: the title card, the two cakes and the five children appear
marks.ten: a second table with ten children appears
marks.ask: a question mark appears over the second table

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about cakes shared in Ruhee's group.
<bookmark mark='ten'/>In the group, two cakes are divided equally among five children. Another group has ten children.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How many cakes does it need, so each child gets the same amount of cake as Ruhee?

beats.on_screen: the two tables stay on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

beats.on_screen: the two cakes cut and shared among the five children of Ruhee's group; each child holds the same piece

marks.share: the two cakes are cut and every child in Ruhee's group gets an equal piece
marks.group: a frame is drawn round the two cakes and the five children together

narration: <bookmark mark='share'/>In Ruhee's group, each child gets an equal piece of the two cakes.
<bookmark mark='group'/>Two cakes and five children together make one sharing group.

beats.on_screen: Given: 2 cakes shared equally among 5 children; another group of 10 children
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, two cakes among five children, and another group of ten children.

beats.on_screen: To find: the number of cakes so that each of the 10 children gets as much as Ruhee

marks.find: the question to find is written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the cakes for ten children, with the same share as Ruhee.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: 10 children is 2 groups of 5 children

marks.two: the ten children split into two groups of five

narration: <bookmark mark='two'/>Step one, ten children make two groups of five children, because five and five make ten.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: each group of 5 needs 2 cakes, so 2 groups need 2 + 2 = 4 cakes

marks.each: two cakes are placed with each group of five
marks.sum: 2 + 2 = 4 is written and four cakes are counted

narration: <bookmark mark='each'/>Step two, each group of five needs two cakes, because that is how Ruhee's group shares.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>Two groups need two plus two, which is four cakes.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: 4 cakes among 10 children, each child gets 4/10 of a cake, the same share as 2/5

marks.tenths: four cakes among ten children are shown, each child holds 4/10
marks.same: the share 4/10 is placed beside Ruhee's share 2/5

narration: <bookmark mark='tenths'/>Step three, four cakes among ten children gives each child four tenths of a cake.
<bookmark mark='same'/>Both groups are shared in the same way, so this is the same share as two fifths.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 4 cakes; each child gets 4/10 = 2/5, so 2/5 = 4/10.

marks.pay: the answer is written and boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='pay'/>Four cakes are needed, and each child gets four tenths, the same as two fifths.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: 7 cakes, because 5 more children need 5 more cakes; seven cakes appear for ten children and each share grows larger than Ruhee's; the bubble is struck out

marks.doubt: Keeko's bubble about five more cakes appears
marks.seven: seven cakes appear for ten children and each share grows larger than Ruhee's

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks seven cakes, because five more children need five more cakes.
<bookmark mark='seven'/>But with seven cakes, every child would get more than Ruhee.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>Adding the same number to cakes and children does not keep the share the same.
